title: Toussaint Louverture Leads the Haitian Revolution
text:
In August 1791 the enslaved people of Saint-Domingue, France's richest colony, rose in revolt. Among those who joined was Toussaint, a man in his late forties who had been born into slavery and later freed, who could read and had worked as a coachman and steward.

Toussaint, who took the name Louverture, trained his followers into a disciplined army. At first he fought alongside Spain against France. In 1794 the French Republic abolished slavery, and he changed sides. Over the next years he defeated the Spanish, forced a British invasion force to withdraw in 1798, and beat rival leaders within the colony. By 1801 he governed all of Hispaniola and issued a constitution that abolished slavery permanently and named him governor for life.

Napoleon then sent a large expedition under his brother-in-law Leclerc to restore French control. In June 1802 Toussaint was invited to a meeting, seized and shipped to France. As he was taken aboard, he reportedly said that in overthrowing him they had cut down only the trunk of the tree of liberty, which would grow again from roots that were many and deep.

He died in a prison in the Jura mountains in April 1803. Haiti declared independence on January 1, 1804.
lesson: Discipline, patience and a clear vision can build strength out of people the world has written off.
people: Toussaint Louverture, Charles Leclerc, Napoleon Bonaparte
location: Saint-Domingue (modern Haiti) and Fort de Joux, France
source: Toussaint's letters and the Constitution of 1801; C. L. R. James, The Black Jacobins (1938)
